M. Okonkwo · 2026

[ 00 — The premise ]

A fragment shader is a tiny program that runs in parallel for every pixel, on the GPU, sixty times a second. There is no DOM, no layout, no page — just math turning coordinates into colour. This is the one thing a page builder can never give you, so we built a studio around it.

01 / The collection

Six shaders, running live

Each tile is its own WebGL context drawing a screen-filling quad. Click any one to load it onto the big stage and drive its uniforms.

02 / Under the hood

How the lab is wired

01

One quad, raw WebGL

We bind a single full-screen triangle and a fragment program. No three.js, no regl — just gl.drawArrays and a ~300-line helper you can read end to end.

02

Standard uniforms

Every shader receives u_time, u_resolution and u_mouse — the three values you need to make a static formula breathe and respond.

03

Live uniform controls

The sliders on the stage push new float values into the running program between frames. Nothing recompiles; you're tuning the math in real time.

04

Hot-reloading editor

The Live Editor recompiles your GLSL as you type, parses the driver's info log, and points at the exact line that failed.

Write your own pixels.

The editor ships with starter shaders, inline error reporting, and the full uniform set already wired. Change one line and watch the GPU repaint.
